tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PPoPP '23 paper (Schardl and Lee, pp. 189-203, DOI 10.1145/3572848.3577509, cited in the repo README) reports the OpenCilk runtime 4%-26% faster on 1 core and 10%-120% faster on 48 cores (geometric mean, 15 Cilk programs) than the other runtimes; the abstract figures were confirmed twice via search snippets but the PDF hosts (MIT DSpace, cesmix.mit.edu, neboat.mit.edu) do not resolve here, and no artifact repo with code, compiler, flags and CPU model exists, so not A.

corrections.baseline: Intel oneTBB, OpenMP and the Intel Cilk Plus runtime, each reached by OpenCilk's own compiler lowering the same Cilk programs to that runtime (the PMAM 2023 program, seen as a search snippet, says OpenCilk was extended to support Cilk Plus, OpenMP and oneTBB with fewer than 2000 new lines each; the abstract itself says only 'the other runtimes')
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the abstract of 'OpenCilk: A Modular and Extensible Software Infrastructure for Fast Task-Parallel Code' (Schardl and Lee, PPoPP '23, pp. 189-203, DOI 10.1145/3572848.3577509), seen only as search-result snippets; the paper (MIT DSpace handle 1721.1/148273, cesmix.mit.edu, neboat.mit.edu, ACM) was unreachable in this environment, so tables, CPU model, compiler flags and the per-runtime geomeans are unseen. Tier B rests on peer review only; no artifact repository was found (the OpenCilk GitHub org has 14 repos: smallapps and applications are regression tests and examples, nothing labelled as the paper's artifact), so A is not supported. The baselines are not hand-written oneTBB or OpenMP code: the same Cilk source is lowered by OpenCilk's Tapir compiler to call the oneTBB, OpenMP or Cilk Plus runtime, so the comparison isolates the runtime scheduler (cheetah) under a front end the authors built, and a native TBB or OpenMP port could behave differently. The 4%-26% and 10%-120% ranges span the three baselines, so the margin against oneTBB or OpenMP alone is unknown and may be the small end. The authors own the system, so this is first-party-authored though peer reviewed. Cilk Plus is deprecated and gone from current GCC and ICC, so that baseline is historical. The measured runtime lives in the separate OpenCilk/cheetah repository; this repo is the compiler (an LLVM fork adding Tapir and Cilk support), and its README makes no numeric comparison (only 'optimize task-parallel programs more effectively than mainstream compilers'). Weak independent hint, snippet only: Los and Petushkov (arXiv 2410.01222, i7-8700, fine-grained SMT kernels) report their Relic framework 30.1% faster than oneTBB and 21.4% faster than OpenCilk, which implies OpenCilk ahead of oneTBB there (derived, not checked). Licence: LLVM parts are Apache-2.0 with LLVM exception (LICENSE.TXT); MIT_LICENSE.TXT says OpenCilk's modifications are MIT with an OpenCilk Addendum allowing distribution under the LLVM licence instead. Retier once the paper PDF is readable.

Shortcomings for the orchestrator: abstract-snippet-only evidence, baselines are OpenCilk-compiled Cilk programs on other runtimes rather than native TBB/OpenMP code, per-baseline margin unknown, first-party authors, measured runtime is in OpenCilk/cheetah not this repo; benchmark_url set to the DOI cited in the README (not openable here).

tier_reason: README is a one-line assertion ('A super fast lock-free (though not always wait-free) thread pool'); the repo holds only LICENSE, README.md and fast_thread_pool.h, with no benchmark, no numbers and no baseline.

corrections.baseline: None named by the author; std::async, boost::asio::thread_pool and BS::thread_pool are the natural incumbents (inferred by the search agent, never compared)
corrections.caveats: Pure assertion with no numbers and no baseline run; kept as a tier D record only because the author (komrad36) is a known performance-oriented developer. The repo has 5 commits, all on 2021-10-18 and 2021-10-19, no tests and no benchmark. Despite the name, fast_thread_pool.h (183 lines) is not a thread pool: it is an intrusive linked-list MPMC queue of plain void(*)() function pointers with AddWork/RemoveWork; it creates no threads and has no worker loop, futures, arguments or captures, so users must write the workers themselves. AddWork and RemoveWork spin with _mm_pause on a tag bit set in the head/tail pointers, which acts as a short spinlock, so a preempted thread can stall the others (not lock-free in the formal sense despite the README). Every AddWork heap-allocates a node with new and every RemoveWork deletes one. The README's own TODOs say it 'could probably be faster with block queues' and should sleep instead of spinning when idle. The memory-order annotations (S1-S9, L1-L6) are not backed by a proof or test; L4 reads the tail with a relaxed load before reading pHead->m_next with acquire, which looked unproven on weakly ordered CPUs (not analysed further). Not comparable to std::async or BS::thread_pool in features, so any speed claim would need a like-for-like queue benchmark.

notes: Metadata confirmed: MIT, 10 stars, 3 forks, 5 commits, last 2021-10-19 'update consume operations', so abandoned. Shortcomings: no numbers or baseline, it is a function-pointer queue rather than a thread pool, tag-bit spinning means it is not truly lock-free, no tests. Kept at D per keep-and-document rule (not-notable reject avoided).
